THOUGHT: The patient is an elderly man with a lytic manubrial mass 12 years after a substernal hemithyroidectomy. Imaging shows a destructive (lytic) lesion of the manubrium; FNA shows follicular thyroid cells in both the residual neck goiter and the manubrial lesion; histology demonstrates thyroid follicles infiltrating adjacent bone trabeculae. Bone infiltration by thyroid follicles indicates metastatic thyroid tissue (malignant behavior). The long interval from prior surgery is compatible with late metastatic spread from a differentiated thyroid carcinoma. Follicular thyroid carcinoma classically spreads hematogenously to bone and produces lytic metastases; the follicular variant of papillary carcinoma can behave similarly and papillary-type nuclear features may have been noted on pathology, so both are considerations. Benign seeding/ectopic thyroid tissue is less likely because true invasion of bone is demonstrated. Other possibilities (Hürthle-cell/oncocytic carcinoma, an occult primary thyroid malignancy, or very rarely a metastatic tumor mimicking thyroid tissue) are lower probability. Overall the most likely diagnosis is metastatic differentiated thyroid carcinoma (most likely follicular carcinoma) to the manubrium.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma to the manubrium (most likely)  
2. Metastatic follicular-variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (differentiated thyroid carcinoma involving bone)  
3. Metastatic Hürthle (oncocytic) cell thyroid carcinoma to bone  
4. Implanted/ectopic benign thyroid tissue or recurrent substernal goiter with local implantation after prior surgery (iatrogenic seeding) — less likely given bone invasion  
5. Other metastatic malignancy to bone with thyroid-like cytology or misinterpreted thyroid tissue (e.g., metastatic carcinoma with thyroidization or sampling artifact)
ground_truth: Follicular thyroid carcinoma with manubrial invasion
